problem:

{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+2y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),

solve the initial value problem

{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+2y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,t>0.
$$

examples.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
x^2 y'' + xy' + 49 y = 0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)= c_1 \cos(7 \ln{x} )  + c_2\sin(7 \ln{x} ),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
x^2 y'' + xy' + 49 y = 0, \quad y(1) = 0, \quad y'(1) = -7, \quad x > 0.
$$
examples.worked_solution:
We find the constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1) = 0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0 = c_1.
$$

- To apply the condition $y'(1) = -7,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{7}{x}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $y'(1) = -7$ and $c_1 = 0$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}-7 & =7{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x) = -\sin(7 \ln{x} ).
$$

feedback.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+7t{y}^{′}+13y=0,\,t>0.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+7t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+13{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+7\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+13{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+7\lambda +13] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+7\lambda +13 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +13 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +13 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +9)-9+13 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +3 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-3\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-3\pm 2\text{i}.$

Note that:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{-3+2\text{i}} & ={t}^{-3}{e}^{\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)), \\ {t}^{-3-2\text{i}} & ={t}^{-3}{e}^{-\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{-3+2\text{i}}+B{t}^{-3-2\text{i}} \\  & =A{t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B{t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B){t}^{-3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B){t}^{-3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={t}^{-3}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$
